PR #75 — Scaffold a default adjacent.toml in `adj add`

When a config file is meant for a human to open and edit, hand-render it as text so comments, # TODO placeholders, and commented-out optional fields survive — toml::to_string(&struct) would drop every one of them — and write it with std::fs::write behind a !path.exists() guard so you never clobber a file the user already owns.

std::fstomlfile-generation

2026-06-21 · +1552/−6 · View PR

The situation

adj add . used to dead-end when a directory had no adjacent.toml. This PR makes it generate a sensible default instead — filling in name and cmd when it can detect the stack, leaving # TODO guidance when it can't. The generated file's whole reason for existing is that a person opens it next and edits it. So two questions: how do you produce a config file that's friendly to a human editor, and how do you write it to disk without ever overwriting one the user already wrote?

The Rust idea

Rust's toml crate can serialize a struct straight to a config string — toml::to_string(&cfg) — the write-side mirror of the #[derive(Deserialize)] that reads adjacent.toml back in (PR #19). It's the obvious reach, and for a machine-to-machine file it's the right one: faithful, round-trippable, no hand-maintained text.

But to_string serializes data, and a struct holds no comments. Feed it an AppConfig and you get back exactly:

name = "myapp"
cmd = "npm run dev"

No header explaining where the file came from. No # Optional: block showing the fields the user could set. No # TODO next to a value they still need to fill in. For a scaffold, those comments aren't decoration — they're the entire payload. The file is a teaching aid disguised as config.

So the tool for a human-facing config file is the opposite of a serializer: you render the text by hand, comments and all, and treat the struct as something you'll parse the result back into later, not something you serialize from. The cost is that you're now responsible for producing valid TOML yourself — which the PR pins down with a test, below.

In this PR

render builds the file as a string. Every line the user benefits from — the header, the # TODOs, the commented-out optional block — is text serde would never emit:

// crates/adj/src/scaffold.rs
fn render(name: Option<&str>, cmd: Option<&str>) -> String {
    let name_line = match name {
        Some(n) => format!("name = \"{n}\"\n"),
        None => "name = \"app\"  # TODO: set a name (lowercase letters, digits, `-`)\n".to_string(),
    };
    let cmd_line = match cmd {
        Some(c) => format!("cmd = \"{c}\"\n"),
        None => "cmd = \"\"  # TODO: set your dev command, e.g. \"npm run dev\"\n".to_string(),
    };
    format!(
        "# Generated by `adj add` — edit and re-run if needed.\n\
         {name_line}\
         {cmd_line}\
         \n\
         # Optional:\n\
         # port_env = \"PORT\"\n\
         # env_file = \".env.local\"\n\
         # idle_timeout = \"15m\"          # \"30s\" / \"1h\" / \"off\"\n\
         # health_check_url = \"/healthz\"\n"
    )
}

The match name / match cmd is where "known value" and "placeholder with guidance" branch: a detected value renders as a live name = "…" line, an absent one renders as a commented # TODO. A serializer can't express that — there's no struct field that means "leave a note for the human here."

Hand-rendering does put one job on you: emitting valid TOML. The PR's doc comment spells out why this particular template is safe without any escaping logic —

// crates/adj/src/scaffold.rs
/// Render the `adjacent.toml` body. `None` fields become TODO placeholders. Detected commands
/// come from a fixed vocabulary (none contain `"`) and `sanitize_name` guarantees `name` is
/// `[a-z0-9-]`, so no TOML string escaping is needed here.

— and a unit test nails the door shut by parsing the rendered string back through the real toml crate. If a future edit ever produces something that isn't valid TOML, this goes red:

// crates/adj/src/scaffold.rs
assert!(
    toml::from_str::<toml::Value>(&toml).is_ok(),
    "invalid toml: {toml}"
);

That's the safety net that makes hand-rendering defensible: you give up serde's guaranteed-valid output, so you buy it back with a round-trip assertion.

Then the write, in client::add. The whole thing is guarded on the file not already existing:

// crates/adj/src/client.rs
let manifest = canon.join("adjacent.toml");
if !manifest.exists() {
    let scaffold = scaffold::build(&canon);
    std::fs::write(&manifest, &scaffold.toml)
        .with_context(|| format!("writing {}", manifest.display()))?;
    // ... branch on detected name/cmd ...
}

std::fs::write is the one-liner form — open (creating or truncating), write the whole buffer, close, all in a call. The if !manifest.exists() in front of it is the not-clobbering rule: a user who already hand-wrote an adjacent.toml never has it silently replaced by a generated one. (An integration test asserts exactly this — an existing manifest comes back byte-identical after adj add.)

Why it matters

Two traps, one on each side.

Reaching for the serializer feels like the disciplined choice and quietly produces a worse file. toml::to_string(&cfg) is faithful and valid — and strips the comments that were the point. The user opens a two-line file with no hint of what else they can set or what they still need to fill in. Knowing when not to serialize is the actual skill here: struct-to-TOML for data you'll read back by machine, hand-rendered text for a file a human edits next.

Skipping the existence check is the destructive one. std::fs::write truncates — point it at a path that already holds a carefully-tuned manifest and the old contents are gone, no prompt, no backup. The !exists() guard is what keeps a convenience feature from eating the user's work.

One honest caveat: exists()-then-write() is check-then-act, so there's a hair-thin window where the file could appear between the two calls. For an interactive command a person runs at a shell, that window doesn't matter. If you needed it to matter — a concurrent or hostile setting — the atomic form is std::fs::OpenOptions::new().create_new(true), which fails outright if the file already exists rather than checking first. adj add doesn't need it; knowing the upgrade path exists is the point.

Related lessons

  • PR #41 is the sibling technique — it also builds a document with format! string templating, and teaches the raw-string-literal (r#"…"#) mechanics that make a multi-line template readable. This lesson is the decision that sits above that mechanism: why you hand-render a config at all instead of serializing a struct, plus the disk write. #41 is how to template; #75 is when (and how not to clobber).
  • PR #19 is the exact mirror: it reads adjacent.toml back in with #[derive(Deserialize)] and Option fields. #75 writes the file #19 parses — and #19's strict "missing cmd is an error" is what the # TODO: set your dev command placeholder is steering the user away from tripping.
  • PR #22 serializes DTOs to JSON with serde — because that output is consumed by jq, a machine, where a stable derived shape is exactly right. Put next to #75 they're the clean contrast: serialize for machines, hand-render for humans.

Dig deeper

  • std::fs::write — the create-or-truncate one-shot write used here.
  • std::fs::OpenOptions::create_new — the atomic "fail if it already exists" alternative to a separate exists() check.
  • The toml crate — toml::from_str (used in the round-trip test) and toml::to_string (the serializer this PR deliberately doesn't use for generation, because it drops comments).
